title: Guru Nanak's gurpurab
hookLine: the full moon of Katak marks his birth, with lamps, kirtan and langar
last: CHAUR · PRASHAD · HUKAMNAMA · SANGAT · VAISAKHI · NAGAR KIRTAN.

cards: Late autumn, the nights drawing in.
In the days before a particular full moon, if you're up very early in a Sikh neighborhood, you might hear singing in the dark streets: small groups walking house to house at dawn, singing hymns.
On the day itself, gurdwaras fill from morning to midnight. Lamps line the windows and rooftops. Fireworks go up.
And the langar kitchens cook for anyone who comes. It's the birthday of the one who started it all: Guru Nanak.

teach.b: A gurpurab is a Guru's day: purab means a festival or holy day, so it's the Guru's festival. Sikhs keep gurpurabs for the Gurus' births, their martyrdoms, and other great moments.
Guru Nanak's is sometimes called Prakash Purab, the festival of the light's appearing.
It falls on the full moon of Katak, a month in the Indian calendar, usually in November. The celebration builds for days.
An akhand path, an unbroken reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, is often timed to finish on the morning of the gurpurab.
Before it, early-morning processions called prabhat pheris go singing through the streets, and there's often a nagar kirtan.

On the day, kirtan and talks about Guru Nanak's life run all day, lamps are lit, and langar feeds everyone. At Nankana Sahib, in Pakistan, where he was born in 1469, pilgrims gather from across the world.

teach.h: THE SOURCES DIFFER ON THE MONTH.
teach.b: Here's an honest detail: the sources don't agree on the month of his birth. Some of the early janamsakhis, the life stories, place it in the spring month of Vaisakh, and some historians follow them.

The Bala janamsakhi gives the full moon of Katak, and that's the date the Sikh community celebrates. Sikhs have discussed this at length, and the celebration in Katak remains. What nobody disputes is what the day is for.
Bhai Gurdas, in his first Var, says that when the true Guru Nanak appeared, the mist cleared and light spread through the world. The lamps say it without words.
And Sikhs say that light didn't go out: it passed through the ten Gurus and rests now in the Granth.

how: Sikhs celebrate Guru Nanak's gurpurab on the full moon of Katak with an akhand path, early-morning prabhat pheris, a nagar kirtan, a full day of kirtan, lamps and langar.

practice: If you can safely, light a candle or a small lamp, or switch on one soft light and turn off the others, and let the flame be the only thing you watch.

Think of one thing you've learned from Guru Nanak on this path: one God, honest work, sharing, the Name remembered, everyone equal at one table. If you pray, you can give thanks; if not, simply honor the light.
